steps.title: A kiosk with separate jobs
steps.display: Cell parts do different jobs.
working: The parts work together in one living unit.
steps.narration: Think of a kiosk at the market. One person keeps records while another packs goods. Your cell also shares out the work.

steps.title: Cell surface membrane
steps.display: Selectively permeable boundary
working: The membrane separates the cell from its surroundings.
It controls exchange between the cell and its surroundings.
steps.narration: A cell needs a border because its contents must stay different from the outside. Think of a compound gate that admits some visitors. In a cell, the thin gate is the membrane.

steps.title: Nucleus and cytoplasm
steps.display: Nucleus holds most of a eukaryotic cell’s DNA.
working: DNA carries genetic information.
Many cell reactions occur in the cytoplasm.
steps.narration: You need instructions before you can make anything reliably. Picture a tailor checking a pattern before cutting cloth. The nucleus holds most of the cell’s instructions, while much of the work goes on around it.

steps.title: Ribosomes and proteins
steps.display: Ribosomes make proteins.
working: Ribosomes can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
steps.narration: Cells need proteins because proteins do jobs such as speeding up reactions. For example, salivary cells need proteins that help digest starch. A ribosome is the tiny structure that assembles such proteins from their building blocks.

steps.title: Mitochondria and ATP
steps.display: Mitochondria are the principal sites of aerobic respiration in eukaryotic cells.
working: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen.
ATP transfers usable energy to cell processes.
steps.narration: You need a way to pay for cell work. A working muscle, for example, cannot contract without an energy supply. We call the small energy carrier ATP, and mitochondria help keep that supply going.

steps.title: Chloroplasts and light
steps.display: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in green plant cells.
working: Chlorophyll absorbs light that helps drive sugar production.
steps.narration: Light is useful because it supplies the energy for making sugars. Think of a green bean leaf in the sun. Look for the green material that catches the light. That material is chlorophyll, inside the chloroplasts.

steps.title: Plant cell wall
steps.display: The plant cell wall contains cellulose.
working: The wall lies outside the cell membrane and gives support.
steps.narration: A plant cell needs something firm around its thin boundary. Think of the sides of a basket holding their shape. Cellulose provides much of that support in a plant wall, which sits outside the softer membrane.

steps.title: Central vacuole
steps.display: A large central vacuole is typical of a mature plant cell.
working: The vacuole holds cell sap.
Water in the vacuole helps keep the cell turgid.
steps.narration: A leafy shoot needs support even where it has no wood. Think of how a wilting leaf can firm up when it takes in water. The full sac inside each cell helps press its contents outwards.

steps.title: Read the mature plant cell
steps.display: Large vacuole → cytoplasm and nucleus often lie near the edge.
working: Locate the wall outside the membrane.
Locate the vacuole inside the cell.
Use the vacuole’s size to explain why much of the cytoplasm forms a thin outer layer.
steps.narration: Why might the nucleus sit off centre? Start with the part taking up most of the room. The space full of sap crowds other contents aside. Then look at the edge of the drawing you have in mind.

steps.title: JAMB 2013 · Match each job to an organelle
steps.display: Which pair contains the principal organelles for aerobic respiration and photosynthesis in a typical green plant cell?
working: Identify the two processes in the order given.
Aerobic respiration points to mitochondria.
Photosynthesis points to chloroplasts.
Answer · Mitochondria and chloroplasts
steps.narration: Start with the jobs because the order matters. One job gets usable energy out of food. The other uses light to help make food. Match each job to its place before you look at the pairs.

steps.title: The cell wall and cell membrane are separate
steps.display: Wall outside membrane
working: The cellulose wall supplies support.
The membrane regulates exchange.
steps.narration: The question asks what the outer support is made of. It is easy to picture just one border. Notice that the gate can control crossings even though a firm wall stands farther out. The material asked for belongs to that wall.

steps.title: Do not treat plant cells as photosynthesis-only
steps.display: Green plant cells contain mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.
working: The cell can respire aerobically as well as carry out photosynthesis.
steps.narration: A plant needs usable energy for its own work. So finding the green structures does not mean the other job disappears. In the pair question, say which job uses food and which job makes it before choosing.

steps.title: Remember jobs before names
steps.display: Identify the function before choosing the structure.
working: Support points to the cellulose wall, protein manufacture to ribosomes, and photosynthesis to chloroplasts.
steps.narration: When the options all sound familiar, let the job guide you. Ask what the cell is trying to do. Once you have that, the long label becomes easier to choose, even if the question changes the wording.

quickCheck.stem: Which feature is typical of a mature plant cell?

options.why: Cytoplasm is usually displaced towards the edge by the large central vacuole.

options.text: The nucleus is pushed towards the centre
options.why: The large vacuole often pushes the nucleus away from the centre.
A cellulose wall is characteristic of plant cells.

options.text: The nucleus is small and irregular
options.why: Nuclear size and shape do not reliably identify a plant cell.

steps.title: Pepper aroma by the stove
steps.display: Particles spread from crowded regions.
working: Net movement can occur without a pump.
steps.narration: You smell pepper soup before you reach the pot. Tiny particles have spread through the air. That spreading helps you picture diffusion.

steps.title: Diffusion follows a concentration difference
steps.display: Net particle movement from higher to lower concentration.
working: Particles keep moving randomly.
At equilibrium there is no net movement.
steps.narration: You can smell soup across the room because the scent starts crowded near the pot. Individual particles wander in all directions. While one region holds more, more particles leave it than return. We call that overall spreading diffusion.

steps.title: Osmosis involves water and a membrane
steps.display: Water moves from higher to lower water potential through a selectively permeable membrane.
working: With other conditions equal, dissolved solute lowers water potential.
steps.narration: Water can cross some barriers that hold dissolved particles back. Picture a membrane sachet containing sugar solution in plain water. If the barrier lets only water pass, the package swells. That water transfer is osmosis.

steps.title: Plant cells respond with turgor or plasmolysis
steps.display: Water entry → turgor. Sufficient water loss → plasmolysis.
working: Turgor develops as cell contents press against the wall.
During plasmolysis, the membrane pulls away from the wall.
steps.narration: The wall matters because it limits how far a plant cell can expand. Think of a leaf that firms up when it takes up water. Its contents push outwards. With enough water loss, those contents can instead shrink away from the wall.

steps.title: Active transport requires energy
steps.display: Transport against a concentration gradient uses energy and a membrane transport protein.
working: Root cells can take up a mineral ion even when its concentration is already higher inside.
steps.narration: Sometimes a cell still needs a substance after the inside is more crowded. Picture a root collecting scarce mineral ions. These ions will not pile up inside by simply spreading out. The cell uses an energy-powered transport system to keep taking them in.

steps.title: Track water in a living plant cell
steps.display: A living plant cell in a sufficiently concentrated external solution loses water.
working: Compare water potential inside and outside.
Water leaves through the plasma membrane.
The cell contents shrink and may pull away from the wall.
steps.narration: Start with the outside because it determines which way water tends to go. A strong surrounding solution leaves less freely available water there. Watch the soft contents retreat. The firm boundary is still there, so the gap is the clue.

steps.title: JAMB 2018 · Name the bursting of red blood cells
steps.display: Red blood cells placed in distilled water swell and burst. What is this bursting called?
working: Distilled water has higher water potential than the cell contents.
Water enters by osmosis.
The red cells swell and burst.
Answer · Haemolysis
steps.narration: The important clue is that the cells break open. First ask what crosses their boundary when they meet pure water. There is no rigid wall to limit expansion. Choose the word for the bursting itself, after you have identified the cause.

steps.title: Do not confuse a process with its outcome
steps.display: Osmosis is water movement. Haemolysis is the bursting of red cells.
working: Plasmolysis describes plant cell contents withdrawing from the cell wall.
steps.narration: One event can have two useful labels. When a red cell takes in water and splits, ask which event the examiner names. Look for the verb that describes the outcome before choosing a word for the cause.

steps.title: Keep a neutral water balance separate from shrinkage
steps.display: Hypertonic outside → net water loss. Isotonic outside → no net water movement.
working: A decrease in cell size shows net loss of water.
steps.narration: Water molecules can still cross in both directions. The question tells you the cell gets smaller, so compare the totals in each direction. When the totals balance, the cell does not shrink for this reason.

steps.title: Check the substance, barrier and energy
steps.display: Track what moves and what drives it.
working: Diffusion is passive, osmosis is passive water movement through a selective membrane, and active transport uses energy.
steps.narration: Ask three questions in your head. What is moving? Is there a barrier that lets water through? Is the cell spending energy to push material uphill? Those clues let you choose the right process when the examples change.

quickCheck.stem: Which solution causes a living animal cell to lose water and shrink?

options.why: A hypotonic solution tends to make an animal cell gain water.
An isotonic solution causes no net water movement across the cell membrane.
Deionized water is hypotonic to a typical animal cell and tends to make it swell.
A hypertonic solution draws water out of the cell, so it shrinks.

steps.title: Sorting at the market
steps.display: Classification groups organisms by shared features.
working: A group can contain smaller groups.
steps.narration: At the market, you can put fruits together, then separate mangoes from oranges. We also sort living things into groups inside bigger groups.

steps.title: Taxonomic ranks narrow the group
steps.display: Kingdom → phylum or division → class → order → family → genus → species
working: Species is the most specific rank in this sequence.
steps.narration: A big group helps you start, but it cannot tell you exactly what you found. Think of narrowing a search from a state to one street. In classification, each step down the list gives you a more specific group.

steps.title: Binomial names use two words
steps.display: Genus name + specific epithet
working: Begin the genus with a capital and the second word with lowercase.
Italicise both words in print.
steps.narration: Common names can differ across places, so scientists use a shared naming system. Look at Homo sapiens as an example. The first word groups us with close relatives. The second completes the name of our species.

steps.title: Recognise the school five-kingdom scheme
steps.display: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia
working: In this historical scheme, Monera contains prokaryotes, which lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
steps.narration: You will meet older group names in JAMB questions. If the question says Monera, picture a typical bacterium. Its main DNA lies in a region without a nuclear membrane. That cell feature tells you why it went into this group.

steps.title: Mammary glands identify mammals
steps.display: Mammals have mammary glands that produce milk for their young.
working: Habitat by itself does not identify a vertebrate class.
steps.narration: An animal can live in water and still belong to the same broad group as a goat. Think of a mother whale feeding her calf. The milk tells you far more about its class than the water around it.

steps.title: Euglena belongs with protists in the syllabus scheme
steps.display: The JAMB syllabus lists Euglena under Protista.
working: Euglena has chloroplasts. Some species can also obtain organic food when light is scarce.
steps.narration: One feature can send you in the wrong direction. Green Euglena can use light like a plant. Yet it is a single cell with other ways of getting food. Use the whole organism and the classification system named in the question.

steps.title: Read a scientific name
steps.display: Homo sapiens identifies a species in the genus Homo.
working: Read Homo first for the genus.
Read sapiens as the specific epithet.
Use the two words together as the full species name.
steps.narration: Why keep both words? The first tells you the group of close relatives. There can be more than one species in that group. Read both together when you want the exact organism named here.

steps.title: JAMB 2012 · Choose the narrowest rank
steps.display: Which listed taxonomic rank is the most specific?
working: Arrange the given ranks from broad to narrow.
Class → family → genus → species.
The last rank in that sequence is the most specific.
Answer · Species
steps.narration: The question asks how tightly you can group the organisms. Imagine starting with a broad folder and opening smaller folders inside it. Compare only the ranks you are given. The one with the narrowest membership is the answer here.

steps.title: Water is not evidence of a fish
steps.display: Whales are mammals and have mammary glands.
working: A shared habitat does not imply a shared class.
Dogfish, sharks and catfish lack mammary glands.
steps.narration: A watery setting can pull your eye towards the fish choices. Instead, ask what the young feed on. Look for the inherited feature that marks a mammal. That clue still works when the animal spends its whole life at sea.

steps.title: Do not stop at genus
steps.display: A genus can contain more than one species.
working: The question seeks the most specific listed rank.
steps.narration: A genus can feel specific because it comes near the end of the list. Think of it as a folder that may still hold several names. Keep narrowing until you reach the rank that names the group more precisely.

steps.title: Use features rather than habitat
steps.display: Classify by the defining features of the group.
working: A milk-producing whale is a mammal even though it is aquatic.
steps.narration: When you meet an unfamiliar animal, you can still work from a strong clue. Ask what body feature the question gives you. Use that feature to choose a group. You can then check whether the option fits the whole description.

quickCheck.stem: Which of these aquatic animals has mammary glands?

options.why: A dogfish is a cartilaginous fish and lacks mammary glands.
A whale is a mammal. Females produce milk for their calves.
Sharks are cartilaginous fish and do not produce milk from mammary glands.
Catfish are bony fish and lack mammary glands.

steps.title: The green leaf’s kitchen
steps.display: Light powers sugar production in green leaves.
working: Leaves use carbon dioxide and water.
steps.narration: Imagine a tiny kitchen in a bean leaf. Sunlight supplies the power. The leaf uses water and a gas from the air to make sugar.

steps.title: Photosynthesis stores energy in sugars
steps.display: Carbon dioxide + water → sugar + oxygen in the overall process with light.
working: Chlorophyll absorbs light in chloroplasts.
Carbon dioxide can enter a leaf through stomata.
steps.narration: A plant needs a supply of sugars to build and run its tissues. Think of a green leaf in sunlight. It can take in a gas through tiny pores. Light provides the energy for turning carbon from that gas into food.

steps.title: Light-dependent reactions split water
steps.display: Light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes.
working: Splitting water releases oxygen.
These reactions supply ATP and NADPH to the Calvin cycle.
steps.narration: The next stage needs both energy and help adding electrons. Think of a leaf just as the sun comes out. Light can drive the first stage. Keep your eye on the water too, because it supplies the oxygen that escapes.

steps.title: The Calvin cycle uses carbon dioxide
steps.display: Light-independent reactions incorporate carbon dioxide into organic molecules.
working: They use ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
Reduction involves gaining electrons in the pathway that produces sugar building blocks.
steps.narration: We care about this stage because it gets carbon from the air into food. Picture a growing leaf making material for new cells. The cycle uses the supplies prepared earlier. Its name tells you it needs no light directly, even though it relies on those supplies.

steps.title: Iodine indicates starch
steps.display: A blue-black iodine result indicates starch.
working: Starch in a leaf can be evidence of photosynthesis under suitable test conditions.
steps.narration: Why use a colour change? Starch in a leaf is hard to pick out by eye. Think of testing a piece of leaf with iodine. A dark blue-black patch gives you a clue that starch is there.

steps.title: Read the overall photosynthesis equation
steps.display: 6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O → C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6O_{2} with light and chlorophyll
working: Read the substances on the left as inputs.
Read glucose and oxygen on the right as products.
Light supplies energy and chlorophyll helps absorb it.
steps.narration: Look at the arrow before naming anything. It separates what the plant starts with from what the process gives back. Light helps drive the change, but it does not supply the carbon. Check the left side to see where that carbon comes from.

steps.title: JAMB 2015 · Identify the light-absorbing pigments
steps.display: Which pair consists of pigments that help capture light in photosynthesis?
working: Look for substances that absorb light during photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll is a photosynthetic pigment.
Carotenoids also absorb light used in photosynthesis.
Answer · Chlorophyll and carotenoids
steps.narration: Why does the word pigment matter? It asks for material that can catch particular colours of light. One choice names a whole organelle. Look inside that organelle instead. Find the pair that can help gather light for the leaf.

steps.title: Keep water splitting and carbon reduction apart
steps.display: Water splitting belongs to the light reactions. Carbon reduction belongs to the Calvin cycle.
working: Light-independent does not mean the process can continue without the products of the light reactions.
steps.narration: Take a moment to name the starting material in each option. If it is water being split, you are looking at the first set of reactions. If carbon is being built into food, look to the later stage. That distinction removes the tempting choices.

steps.title: A chloroplast is not a pigment
steps.display: A chloroplast is an organelle. Chlorophyll and carotenoids are pigments.
working: A pigment absorbs particular wavelengths of light.
steps.narration: Read the kind of object the question wants. A whole organelle is like the place where the work happens. A pigment is one of the materials that catches light there. Choosing the place would miss the type of answer requested.

steps.title: Follow the two stages in order
steps.display: Light capture supplies the Calvin cycle.
working: Light reactions release oxygen from water. The Calvin cycle uses carbon dioxide to make sugar building blocks.
steps.narration: If you forget the names, follow the jobs. The first stage gathers energy and produces supplies. The second uses them to build food from carbon in the air. You can place the details back in order from those two jobs.

quickCheck.stem: Which process takes place during the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis?

options.why: Water is oxidised during the light-dependent reactions.
Photolysis is light-driven splitting of water in the light-dependent reactions.
The carbon entering through carbon dioxide is reduced on its way to sugar building blocks.
The Calvin cycle pathway uses energy and reducing power to convert carbon dioxide into organic molecules.

steps.title: Making yam easier to use
steps.display: Digestion breaks food into small molecules that can be absorbed.
working: Chewing breaks up food before enzymes act on it.
steps.narration: Think about chewing boiled yam. The pieces get smaller. Inside you, tiny helpers called enzymes keep breaking food down until your body can take it in.

steps.title: Mechanical digestion exposes more surface
steps.display: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces.
working: Smaller pieces expose more surface for digestive enzymes.
Chemical digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller molecules.
steps.narration: Enzymes work where they can touch the food. Compare one lump of yam with that same lump after you chew it. Smaller pieces give the enzymes more surface to reach. The chewing itself has not changed starch into sugar.

steps.title: Amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth
steps.display: Ptyalin is another name for salivary amylase.
working: It begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates.
Stomach acidity greatly reduces its activity.
steps.narration: Why start in the mouth? Starch is already meeting saliva as you chew. A bite of cooked yam gives the enzyme something to work on. When the mixture reaches the much more acidic stomach, that enzyme works poorly.

steps.title: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach
steps.display: Pepsin breaks proteins into shorter peptides.
working: The stomach’s acidic conditions help activate pepsin and favour its action.
steps.narration: Large proteins need to be cut before their building blocks can be absorbed. Think of protein from a piece of fish. In the stomach, acid helps an enzyme begin cutting that protein into shorter chains called peptides.

steps.title: Bile and lipase do different jobs
steps.display: Bile breaks large fat droplets into smaller droplets.
working: Smaller droplets expose more surface for lipase.
Lipase breaks down fats chemically.
steps.narration: Imagine oily stew with large drops on top. Breaking each drop into smaller ones gives the enzyme more places to act. Bile does that first job. The fat-digesting enzyme, lipase, then breaks up the molecules themselves.

steps.title: Villi make absorption more efficient
steps.display: The small intestine has many villi that increase the surface for absorption.
working: Most digested nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
steps.narration: Digestion is only useful if the products can get into your body. Think of glucose from yesterday’s yam. Much of it can enter the blood through the intestinal lining. Tiny projections called villi give that lining more room for transfer.

steps.title: Follow starch from cooked yam
steps.display: Starch → smaller sugars → glucose for absorption
working: Chewing exposes more of the yam to saliva.
Salivary amylase starts breaking starch down.
Further digestion in the small intestine produces glucose for absorption.
steps.narration: Start with the obstacle. A large starch molecule is too big to take up whole. You can see what chewing does, but the smaller chemical changes go on afterwards. Follow the food until its sugars are small enough to cross the lining.

steps.title: JAMB 2013 · Identify the enzyme by its starting material and site
steps.display: Which of these enzymes begins starch digestion in the mouth?
working: The material is starch.
The site is the mouth.
Ptyalin is salivary amylase.
Answer · Ptyalin
steps.narration: Two clues narrow the field. The question tells you where the work begins and what it acts on. Lipase points to fat. Pepsin points to protein. Find the name for the starch enzyme that meets your food as you chew.

steps.title: Separate digestion from nutrient absorption
steps.display: Pancreatic enzymes digest fats, proteins and carbohydrates.
working: Vitamins and minerals are absorbed without being broken down by pancreatic digestive enzymes.
Humans lack enzymes that digest cellulose.
steps.narration: If a substance is useful, that does not mean it needs cutting up first. Vitamins and minerals illustrate that difference. And look closely at cellulose. It is a carbohydrate, but you do not make a digestive enzyme that cuts it up.

steps.title: Do not choose the familiar stomach enzyme
steps.display: Ptyalin acts on starch in the mouth. Pepsin acts on protein in the stomach.
working: Check both the food molecule and the site.
steps.narration: You may remember pepsin quickly because it comes up often. Pause and ask what it cuts. A protein enzyme does not solve a starch question. Then check that the place named is where the enzyme first meets the food.

steps.title: Match the enzyme to its food molecule
steps.display: Substrate helps identify the enzyme.
working: Amylase acts on starch, pepsin acts on protein, and lipase acts on fats.
steps.narration: A list of enzyme names can feel like guesswork. Ask what needs breaking down first. Then check where the enzyme meets that food. Those two clues help you choose the right name without memorising a long list in order.

quickCheck.stem: Which set lists the major food substances digested by enzymes from the human pancreas?

options.why: The pancreas supplies lipase for fats, protein-digesting enzymes and amylase for starch.
Vitamins need no pancreatic digestion and human enzymes do not digest cellulose.
Vitamins are nutrients to absorb, rather than targets of pancreatic digestive enzymes.
Minerals need no chemical digestion and human pancreatic enzymes do not digest cellulose.

steps.title: Carrying supplies
steps.display: Transport moves materials to cells.
working: Animals use blood. Vascular plants use xylem and phloem.
steps.narration: A market rider carries supplies to different shops. Your blood carries supplies around you. Plants also have routes for moving water and food.

steps.title: Xylem carries water and mineral ions
steps.display: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots.
working: Water loss at leaves helps pull water up through xylem.
steps.narration: A tall plant cannot rely on water drifting from one cell to the next for the whole journey. Think of rainwater taken up by maize roots. As leaves lose water, a connected column can be pulled upwards through narrow tubes.

steps.title: Phloem moves sugars between sources and sinks
steps.display: Phloem moves sugars from a source to a sink.
working: A source releases sugar for transport.
A sink uses or stores it.
steps.narration: Growing parts need food even when they make little of it. Picture sugars leaving a green leaf for a developing root. Call the sending part a source. The receiving part, which uses or stores the sugar, is a sink.

steps.title: The heart drives two circuits
steps.display: Right ventricle → lungs. Left ventricle → body.
working: Blood returns from the lungs to the left side of the heart.
Blood returns from body tissues to the right side.
steps.narration: Your heart sends blood on two journeys because it needs to visit the lungs as well as the rest of you. Trace a delivery route with your finger. Start at the heart. After the lungs, come back to the left side before tracing the longer trip.

steps.title: Vessels differ by direction and exchange
steps.display: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry it back.
working: Thin capillary walls facilitate exchange with tissues.
steps.narration: Use direction because oxygen content can mislead you. The vessel leaving the right side for the lungs is still an artery. Once inside a tissue, look for tiny vessels with thin walls. That is where transfer can take place.

steps.title: Blood components have different functions
steps.display: Red cells carry oxygen. White cells help defend the body.
working: Platelets help form clots.
Plasma carries many dissolved substances.
steps.narration: Whole blood does several jobs, so ask what the body needs at that moment. If you scrape a knee, for instance, small fragments called platelets gather at the damaged spot. They help stop the bleeding. Oxygen delivery is a different job.

steps.title: Follow oxygen-rich blood to a leg muscle
steps.display: Lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → leg capillaries
working: After gas exchange, follow the return from the lungs.
Trace the blood through the left side of the heart.
Leave by the aorta and reach a capillary bed in the leg.
steps.narration: Why return to the heart after the lungs? The blood needs another push to reach your leg. Trace the vessel that brings it back. Then follow the chamber that sends it out again. At the small vessels, oxygen can reach the working tissue.

steps.title: JAMB 2010 · Identify the chamber that drives systemic circulation
steps.display: Which chamber supplies the force that drives blood into the main body circulation?
working: Systemic circulation serves the tissues other than the lungs.
The left ventricle pumps into the aorta.
Arteries and veins are vessels rather than pumping chambers.
Answer · Left ventricle
steps.narration: Start at the destination in the question. The blood is going around the body, so leave the lung route aside. Trace back from the large artery to the muscle chamber behind it. That chamber provides the push the examiner is asking about.

steps.title: Avoid swapping the plant transport tissues
steps.display: Xylem carries root water and mineral ions. Phloem distributes sugars.
working: Cambium makes new vascular tissues during secondary growth.
The cortex is not the main long-distance conducting tissue.
steps.narration: Several plant tissues sound plausible if you only remember their names. Ask what has been loaded into the route. Here it is water with soil minerals. That leads you to the tubes carrying water upwards, before you think about where sugars go.

steps.title: Do not mistake a vessel for a chamber
steps.display: The left ventricle drives systemic circulation.
working: An artery carries blood away from the heart but does not replace a pumping chamber.
steps.narration: Both vessels and chambers carry blood, so the wording matters. Look for the part whose muscular squeeze sends blood out. Once you identify that push, follow the destination. A route towards the lungs would point to the other ventricle.

steps.title: Follow the load and destination
steps.display: Name the cargo before naming its route.
working: In plants, distinguish water and mineral ions from sugars. In animals, use blood flow direction and destination.
steps.narration: When transport questions feel tangled, give your finger a starting point. Say what is travelling and where it is headed. Then trace the route and pick the tissue, vessel or chamber that would actually carry it that way.

quickCheck.stem: Which plant tissue carries water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots?

options.why: Vascular cambium produces new xylem and phloem during secondary growth rather than conducting the main water stream.
Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals from the roots.
The cortex is ground tissue. It is not the main long-distance route for this cargo.
Phloem chiefly transports sugars and other organic solutes from sources to sinks.

steps.title: Fuel for the football game
steps.display: Cells release usable energy from food.
working: Muscles use that energy to do work.
steps.narration: After eating, you can run after a football. Your cells unlock some energy stored in food so your muscles can work.

steps.title: ATP transfers energy to cell work
steps.display: Cellular respiration captures usable energy in ATP.
working: Breathing brings in air. Cellular respiration is a chemical process inside cells.
steps.narration: Getting air into your chest helps because your tissues need oxygen. The work still happens inside your cells. When you kick a football, your muscle needs an energy carrier it can use immediately. We call that carrier ATP.

steps.title: Aerobic respiration depends on oxygen
steps.display: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Energy is transferred to ATP.
working: Glycolysis starts glucose breakdown in the cytosol.
Later stages of aerobic respiration in a typical eukaryotic cell involve the mitochondria.
steps.narration: Oxygen matters because it lets the cell finish gathering much more usable energy from its fuel. Think of a leg muscle during a steady walk. The first stage starts in the fluid inside the cell. Much of the later work depends on mitochondria.

steps.title: Yeast fermentation yields ethanol and carbon dioxide
steps.display: Without oxygen, yeast can produce ethanol and carbon dioxide from sugars.
working: Fermentation lets glycolysis continue.
Energy captured per glucose is much lower than in aerobic respiration.
steps.narration: Yeast still needs a small supply of usable energy when oxygen is unavailable. Think about bubbles that make bread dough rise. The escaping gas is carbon dioxide. Ethanol is another product, even though you mainly notice the bubbles.

steps.title: Muscle cells can form lactate
steps.display: Under conditions of high energy demand, muscles can convert pyruvate to lactate.
working: This lets glycolysis continue.
Lactate formation does not release carbon dioxide in this step.
steps.narration: A fast sprint can demand energy sooner than the aerobic pathway can supply it. Think of chasing a loose ball. Your muscles can keep the first stage going by forming lactate. That is a different outcome from the one you see in bread dough.

steps.title: The Krebs cycle continues fuel breakdown
steps.display: The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix in typical eukaryotic cells.
working: It releases carbon dioxide and transfers energy to electron carriers.
steps.narration: Why does the cell need another stage after splitting glucose? Much of the fuel’s energy is still available. Think of a muscle cell on a steady walk. It passes some of that energy to small carriers for use in the next stage.

steps.title: Use bubbles to reason about yeast dough
steps.display: Carbon dioxide from yeast can expand a dough bubble.
working: Yeast breaks down sugars without oxygen in fermentation.
The carbon dioxide becomes trapped in the dough.
The expanding bubbles help raise the dough.
steps.narration: Why does the dough get bigger? Follow what fills the holes. Yeast can make a gas as it uses sugar. The gas collects inside the dough, so you can use the rising as a clue even without seeing the individual cells.

steps.title: JAMB 2010 · Find the second product of yeast fermentation
steps.display: When yeast breaks down sugar without oxygen, what is produced along with carbon dioxide?
working: Identify the organism as yeast.
Identify the condition as absence of oxygen.
The question gives carbon dioxide and asks for its companion product.
Answer · Alcohol
steps.narration: The organism and the oxygen clue work together. First settle which pathway fits yeast here. The gas is already named, so set it aside. Think of the other compound formed in that pathway. You need the one associated with yeast rather than muscle cells.

steps.title: Distinguish ATP from its precursors
steps.display: ATP is a direct energy carrier. ADP and AMP are different molecules.
working: Cells can make ATP by adding a phosphate to ADP.
Heat is energy transferred to the surroundings rather than a molecule.
steps.narration: The question asks what the cell can use to pay for work. Look carefully at the endings of those nearly identical names. Extra phosphate changes what the molecule can do. Heat can accompany the process, but it is a different kind of answer.

steps.title: Yeast and muscle give different products
steps.display: Yeast fermentation can yield ethanol. Muscle cells form lactate.
working: The organism in the stem identifies the relevant pathway.
steps.narration: The absence of oxygen is only one clue. Look at the living thing as well. If the question moves from dough to a working muscle, do not carry over the same second product. The pathways end in different compounds.

steps.title: Check the oxygen clue and the organism
steps.display: Oxygen availability and cell type help identify the pathway and products.
working: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen. Yeast fermentation can yield ethanol and carbon dioxide, while muscle cells can form lactate.
steps.narration: Start by asking whether the pathway can use oxygen. Then check which living thing is doing the work. Remember the dough and the sprint. They give you two different clues for the products when the question describes energy release without relying on oxygen.

quickCheck.stem: Which molecule directly captures much of the usable energy released during cellular respiration?

options.why: Heat is energy transferred to the surroundings, not a molecule that couples respiration to cell work.
ADP can accept a phosphate to form ATP. It is not the main energy carrier asked for.
AMP has one phosphate and is not the main direct energy carrier of respiration.
ATP transfers usable energy to processes such as muscle contraction.

steps.title: Messages that tell the body what to do
steps.display: Nerves and hormones help coordinate the body.
working: A quick withdrawal can happen through a reflex.
steps.narration: Touch a hot pot and your hand pulls away quickly. Your body gets messages to the right parts so they can work together.

steps.title: Nerves carry messages along neurones
steps.display: Neurones transmit electrical signals along their membranes.
working: At many synapses, chemical messengers carry a signal from one cell to the next.
steps.narration: A message needs a route so the correct part can respond. Think of turning your head towards a sudden clap. Signals can run along nerve cells. Where one ends, a chemical can cross the small gap to pass the news on.

steps.title: A reflex can act before conscious awareness
steps.display: Receptor → sensory neurone → spinal cord → motor neurone → muscle for a withdrawal reflex.
working: The response can begin before the person is consciously aware of pain.
steps.narration: A quick escape matters when something could hurt you. Think of your finger meeting a hot pot. A short route through the spinal cord lets the muscle get moving while information is still travelling towards the brain.

steps.title: Hormones travel in blood to target cells
steps.display: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood.
working: Target cells respond if they have the appropriate receptors.
steps.narration: Blood reaches many places, so a signal needs a way to select its audience. After a meal, for example, insulin can reach many tissues. Cells respond if they can recognise that message. The recognising structures are called receptors.

steps.title: The cerebellum helps coordinate movement
steps.display: The cerebellum helps coordinate voluntary movement and maintain balance.
working: It fine-tunes movements so that they can be smooth and accurate.
steps.narration: Your muscles need good timing even when you already know what to do. Think of catching a ball as you step sideways. Your balance and hand movement have to fit together. The cerebellum helps make that adjustment.

steps.title: Insulin helps lower blood glucose
steps.display: Rising blood glucose stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells.
working: Insulin promotes glucose uptake in responsive tissues and favours storage as glycogen.
steps.narration: The body needs to deal with glucose entering the blood after food. Think of eating a bowl of rice. Some tissues take up more glucose when they receive the insulin signal. The body can keep some as a stored carbohydrate called glycogen.

steps.title: Trace withdrawal from a hot surface
steps.display: Heat stimulus → skin receptor → spinal cord → arm muscle
working: Heat activates sensory receptors in the skin.
Signals travel into the spinal cord through sensory neurones.
Motor neurones send a signal to the muscles that withdraw the hand.
steps.narration: Why pull back before thinking it through? A delay would keep your skin on the heat. Begin where you felt the danger, then trace the message inwards. Now follow the return journey to the muscle. The short circuit gives you a fast response.

steps.title: JAMB 2014 · Identify the cerebellum’s main job in the options
steps.display: Which function is most closely associated with the cerebellum?
working: Connect the cerebellum with balance and timing of movement.
Distinguish that role from a simple spinal reflex or endocrine control.
Answer · Coordinating muscle activity
steps.narration: Start with the job you could watch. Is the body keeping its balance and making a controlled movement? That is the clue for this brain region. A reflex has a different route. Hormone control points you towards other parts of the brain.

steps.title: Two signalling systems work together
steps.display: Nerves and hormones coordinate mammals.
working: A muscle can respond to a message. It is not a second body-wide signalling system in this question.
steps.narration: Look at the word signalling. A muscle can pull on a bone after a message arrives. The question wants ways to send the messages in the first place. One uses nerve cells. The other sends chemical signals through the blood.

steps.title: Separate coordination from a spinal reflex
steps.display: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and helps maintain balance.
working: In a simple withdrawal reflex, a spinal circuit can trigger the immediate response.
steps.narration: A quick movement alone does not tell you which centre controls it. Picture catching a ball without losing your balance. That takes timing. A hand that pulls away from heat illustrates the short protective circuit asked about in a different question.

steps.title: Ask how the message travels
steps.display: Nerve circuits and circulating hormones coordinate responses.
working: Nervous signals travel along neurones. Blood carries endocrine signals to suitable targets.
steps.narration: When an example feels unfamiliar, follow its message. You can ask if nerve cells carry it along a particular route. Or you can ask if a chemical travels in the blood. That distinction helps you name the type of control.

quickCheck.stem: What two signalling mechanisms coordinate and regulate mammalian body functions?

options.why: Muscles can carry out responses, but this pair leaves out hormonal signalling.
Nervous signals and circulating hormones both help coordinate mammalian functions.
This omits the endocrine signals carried in blood.
This omits the signals sent by neurones.

lessons.title: Ecology, energy flow and nutrient cycles

steps.title: A school garden after rain
steps.display: An ecosystem includes organisms and their non-living surroundings.
working: Organisms interact with each other and with water, soil and air.
steps.narration: After rain, look at a school garden. Plants, insects, wet soil and air all matter. The living things and their surroundings make one system.

steps.title: An ecosystem includes the physical environment
steps.display: Ecosystem = community + non-living environment and their interactions
working: A community includes the populations of different species living in an area.
steps.narration: Knowing which creatures you saw is only part of the picture. In a school garden, insects and plants interact with soil, rain and light. Include the living groups and their surroundings if you want to describe the whole system.

steps.title: Arrows show the direction of food transfer
steps.display: Producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer
working: Arrows point from food to the organism that eats it.
Producers such as green plants use light energy to make organic food.
steps.narration: Start with food because that tells you which way to draw the arrow. Think of a grasshopper chewing grass. The insect gets some of the energy the grass stored. The arrow goes towards the insect because it receives that energy.

steps.title: Less usable energy reaches higher trophic levels
steps.display: Available energy decreases along feeding levels.
working: Organisms use part of what they take in for their own life processes.
Respiration dissipates some energy as heat.
steps.narration: A predator cannot get all the energy its prey once ate. Think of a grasshopper jumping before a bird catches it. The grasshopper has already used some of its food to move. Some of that energy has been released as heat.

steps.title: Carbon transfers between air and organisms
steps.display: Photosynthesis takes up carbon dioxide. Respiration returns carbon dioxide.
working: Feeding transfers carbon in organic matter.
Decomposition and combustion can return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
steps.narration: Carbon keeps changing where it is stored. Picture a growing bean plant. It takes carbon from the air while it makes food. When organisms break down some of that food, carbon can move back into the air as a gas.

steps.title: Different processes move nitrogen through the cycle
steps.display: Fixation converts nitrogen gas into reduced nitrogen compounds.
working: Nitrification produces nitrite and then nitrate from ammonium.
Denitrification returns nitrogen gas to the atmosphere.
steps.narration: Plants need nitrogen to build useful molecules, yet the gas in the air is hard for most organisms to use. Think of a bean root with nodules. Some bacteria there turn the gas into a form that can enter living matter.

steps.title: Water cycles between surfaces, air and land
steps.display: Evaporation and transpiration add water vapour to the air.
working: Cooling can cause condensation.
Precipitation returns water to the surface.
steps.narration: A puddle can disappear without a person taking any water away. The water enters the air as vapour. If moist air cools, drops can form. Follow where the water goes rather than thinking that the puddle’s water has been destroyed.

steps.title: Track a producer and two consumers
steps.display: Grass → grasshopper → insect-eating bird
working: Grass makes organic food and is the producer.
The grasshopper feeds directly on grass and is a primary consumer.
The bird that eats the grasshopper is a secondary consumer.
steps.narration: Count feeding steps from the plant. The insect gets its food straight from the producer, so it takes the first consumer spot. The bird must go through the insect to get that food energy. That places it one step further along.

steps.title: JAMB 2016 · Identify the change specific to the nitrogen cycle
steps.display: Which listed process belongs directly to the nitrogen cycle rather than the carbon cycle?
working: Look for a compound carrying the element named in the question.
Nitrate is a nitrogen compound.
Photosynthesis moves carbon dioxide into organic matter.
Answer · Formation of nitrates
steps.narration: First check the element in the product. Decomposition can take part in more than one cycle, so its name alone will not settle the choice. Look instead for a form of nitrogen that does not belong to the carbon pathway.

steps.title: Do not confuse fixation with nitrification
steps.display: Nitrogen fixation starts with nitrogen gas. Nitrification acts on reduced nitrogen already in the soil.
working: Denitrification can take nitrogen from nitrate back to nitrogen gas.
steps.narration: You can get this right by circling the starting material. The question starts in the air with a gas, so look for the step that makes it usable by organisms. A step that begins with ammonium is further along the route.

steps.title: Separate nitrate formation from decomposition
steps.display: Nitrification forms nitrate. Decomposition can affect both carbon and nitrogen cycles.
working: Use the element in the named product to distinguish the processes.
steps.narration: Dead matter contains more than one element, so breaking it down can feed several cycles. The question asks you to pick a clue tied to one cycle specifically. Focus on the compound being formed and identify the element in it.

steps.title: Track energy and matter differently
steps.display: Energy flows through food chains. Nutrients cycle between organisms and their surroundings.
working: Organisms keep receiving energy while carbon and nitrogen can return to the environment and be used again.
steps.narration: When a question says something moves, ask whether it is energy or material. You can trace a carbon atom into a leaf and back to the air. Energy used in that leaf can leave as heat. Keep those journeys separate.

quickCheck.stem: Which group of soil microorganisms can convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds that enter living systems?

options.why: Putrefying bacteria decompose organic matter and can release ammonium from it.
Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium or nitrite. They do not start with gaseous nitrogen.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into reduced compounds such as ammonia.
Denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into gases such as nitrogen and return them to the atmosphere.

steps.title: One bean from each bowl
steps.display: An offspring receives one allele for a gene from each parent.
working: The pair can affect what trait you observe.
steps.narration: Imagine picking one bean from each of two bowls. The two picks make a pair. A young plant gets one version of a gene from each parent.

steps.title: Genotype and phenotype describe different things
steps.display: Genotype is the allele combination. Phenotype is the observable trait.
working: With complete dominance, AA and Aa show the dominant phenotype.
The recessive phenotype appears in aa.
steps.narration: What you see cannot always tell you both gene versions. Think of Mendel’s round peas. A round seed can have two copies of the round version or only one. The seed shape looks alike even though the pairs differ.

steps.title: Mendel’s law of segregation
steps.display: An allele pair separates during gamete formation.
working: In a simple Aa model, gametes receive A or a with equal probability.
steps.narration: Every new pair needs one contribution from each parent. Picture a pea plant with two versions of the gene for seed shape. Each egg or pollen cell gets just one version. That separation is why a cross has different possible outcomes.

steps.title: Independent assortment applies to unlinked genes
steps.display: Alleles of unlinked genes assort independently into gametes.
working: A monohybrid cross tracks one gene and uses segregation directly.
Closely linked genes can depart from independent assortment.
steps.narration: Separate two traits in your mind before combining them. Mendel considered pea seed colour and shape together. For unlinked genes, a gamete’s version for colour need not tell you its version for shape. A one-trait question needs only one pair.

steps.title: A Punnett square combines possible gametes
steps.display: Aa × Aa → AA, Aa, Aa, aa
working: Each parent can contribute A or a.
In the simple complete dominance model, the genotype ratio is 1 to 2 to 1.
steps.narration: You can easily miss a pairing in your head. Put the contributions where you can see them. For example, either parent could supply the small-letter version. Work through each pairing once, even when two pairings give the same result.

steps.title: Work Mendel’s seed-shape cross
steps.display: Rr × Rr → RR, Rr, Rr, rr
working: Let R represent round and r represent wrinkled in the simple pea model.
List R and r as possible gamete alleles for each parent.
Pair each allele from the first parent with each from the second.
RR and both Rr outcomes are round. rr is wrinkled.
Expected phenotype ratio is 3 round to 1 wrinkled.
steps.narration: Why count two mixed pairs? They come from different contributions, even though they look the same. Start with what each parent can pass on. Pair the choices one at a time. Only then count the seed shapes. The order keeps the two ratios apart.

steps.title: JAMB 2012 · Use the maize ratio to identify the dominant trait
steps.display: A cross between two yellow-seeded maize plants yields yellow and white seeds in a 3 to 1 ratio. What does that suggest about yellow in a simple monohybrid model?
working: Two yellow plants produced some white seeds.
Occurrence of white is consistent with each yellow parent contributing a recessive allele.
A heterozygote cross gives an expected 3 to 1 phenotype ratio.
Answer · A dominant trait
steps.narration: Start with the surprising seeds in the question. Two yellow parents can produce a white outcome. Both must be able to pass on the version whose effect is hidden in them. Then check that the ratio fits this explanation.

steps.title: Do not count a carrier as expressing the recessive trait
steps.display: AA and Aa show the dominant phenotype. Only aa shows the recessive phenotype.
working: Two mixed allele combinations occur in the square. Neither expresses the recessive phenotype under complete dominance.
steps.narration: Look carefully at what the question asks you to count. Seeing a small letter anywhere does not mean its effect is visible. Check each pair for two copies of the recessive version before putting it in the count.

steps.title: Use inheritance to infer dominance
steps.display: In the maize cross, the two yellow parents produce a white recessive phenotype.
working: Under the stated model, a 3 to 1 ratio from two yellow parents supports yellow dominance.
steps.narration: The strongest clue is the pair of parents, not just the number of yellow seeds. Both parents look yellow but can pass on a version for white. Work from that clue before assigning the capital letter in the cross.

steps.title: Count outcomes only after pairing gametes
steps.display: Separate alleles, pair them, then count the requested phenotype.
working: The expected recessive proportion in Aa × Aa with complete dominance is \frac{1}{4}.
steps.narration: When a cross looks confusing, use the same order every time. Work out what each parent can pass on. Combine those possibilities before you decide what is visible. Finally check whether the examiner wants allele pairs or outward traits.

quickCheck.stem: For a single gene with complete dominance, two heterozygous parents are crossed. What fraction of offspring are expected to show the recessive trait?

options.why: This fraction counts the offspring showing the dominant phenotype.
This fraction counts the heterozygotes. Heterozygotes show the dominant phenotype in this model.
One pairing out of four gives two recessive alleles and expresses the recessive phenotype.
Some pairings contain a dominant allele, so the recessive trait cannot appear in all offspring.
